observations:
Torah #261 is a two-sentence practical aphorism. A careful reading of the full source text was conducted to identify any independent domain of 3+ concepts connected by explicit bechina language.

Result: None found.

The word 'בְּחִינַת' does not appear in the text at all. The teaching contains no conceptual equations of the form 'X is an aspect of Y.' The entire structure of the Torah is eitza (causal-practical):

1. A person falls from his level (נְפִילָה מִמַּדְרֵגָה).
2. This was arranged by Heaven so that he would be aroused to draw closer (הִתְרַחֲקוּת → הִתְקָרְבוּת).
3. The practical advice (עֵצָה): begin fresh as if he had never begun (הַתְחָלָה מֵחָדָשׁ).
4. This is a great principle: begin fresh every day.

The phrase 'הִתְרַחֲקוּת – תְּחִלַּת הִתְקָרְבוּת' was examined carefully as a possible bechina candidate. While the aphoristic form resembles an equation, the logical structure is teleological-causal: the distancing is *the beginning of* closeness (i.e., it produces it, it starts the process), not *the same essence as* closeness. 'תְּחִלַּת' (beginning/start-of) is a causal-sequential marker, not an identity marker. If the Rebbe had meant bechina, he would have written 'הִתְרַחֲקוּת הִיא בְּחִינַת הִתְקָרְבוּת' or similar. The absence of bechina language is significant.

Even if the two concepts (הִתְרַחֲקוּת / הִתְקָרְבוּת) were treated as a bechina pair, they would constitute only two concepts — insufficient for a package (which requires a meaningful cluster). No third concept in the text can be joined to them via bechina language.

Conclusion: Torah #261 contains zero bechina relationships in the dataset and zero bechina language in the source text. No packages exist for this Torah, and no new package proposals are warranted. This Torah is purely eitza content — practical spiritual guidance with no conceptual topology to map.
